title: Increased reproductive success of women after prenatal undernutrition.
ehr_evidence: We assessed reproductive success (number of children, number of twins, age at delivery, childlessness) of men and women born around the time of the Dutch famine of 1944–1945 in the Wilhelmina Gasthuis, Amsterdam, whose birth records have been kept. Trained nurses carried out all interviews.
summary: A birth cohort study of 855 participants from the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort (born around the 1944–1945 Amsterdam famine) investigating whether prenatal famine exposure affected reproductive success.
key_findings: Women exposed to famine in utero had more children than unexposed women (mean 2.0 vs 1.7, P = 0.002).
Famine-exposed women were younger at delivery of their first child (23.2 vs 23.7 years, P = 0.05).
Famine-exposed women had more twins (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.1 to 7.0).
Famine-exposed women were less likely to be childless (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.98).
In utero famine exposure did not affect reproductive success of men.
Age at first delivery was reduced in exposed women (unadjusted HR 0.8, adjusted HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.6–1.0).
captured_features: Age at delivery of first child
Duration of delay to first pregnancy
population: Adults aged 58 from the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort born around the 1944–1945 Amsterdam famine (Wilhelmina Gasthuis), Netherlands; 855 participants, 55% women
limitations: Low participation rate (855 of 1423 eligible, 55%), raising selection bias.
Reproductive outcome data were self-reported via interviews.
Genetic confounding could not be fully excluded.
